title: Amazon workers near Vancouver secure historic first union contract
html:
Warehouse workers at YVR2, the Amazon fulfilment centre in Delta, B.C., pictured on Monday, were originally granted union certification by the BC Labour Relations Board in July 2025.Ethan Cairns/The Globe and Mail

Hundreds of warehouse workers at an Amazon.com Inc. AMZN-Q facility near Vancouver have secured their first union contract with Unifor after a lengthy legal battle with the company that spanned almost 18 months.

The 800-odd workers – represented by Unifor, Canada’s largest private-sector union – are now the only group of Amazon workers in the world to be governed by a collective agreement. There are a handful of other Amazon warehouses globally that are unionized, but none have managed to reach a collective agreement with the company.

Unifor’s Western regional director Gavin McGarrigle said in an interview that the union now has a seat at the table to challenge the company on issues such as injuries and worker safety. “This has been a long time coming. We are pleased.”

Amazon, however, is disputing the process that led to the securing of a first contract. In a Nov. 13 statement, the company’s vice-president of global operations, Ofori Agboka, described the way in which Amazon workers obtained their first contract as “improper, unfair” and one that “defies common sense.” He said that some Amazon workers will effectively take home less money than they did before, despite wage increases, because they will have to pay union dues.

A copy of the three-year contract, viewed by The Globe and Mail, states that workers will receive wage increases of 3.25 per cent starting October 2027, and 3.5 per cent starting October 2028. By the end of the contract, on Oct. 31, 2029, most workers will be paid at least $29 an hour. The contract also includes a clause that guarantees unionized workers will receive the same future pay increases that non-union workers receive, if greater than the percentages set out in the contract.

The sequence of events leading up to the agreement is long and complicated, with Unifor repeatedly accusing Amazon of employing stalling tactics to deter a first contract, and the BC Labour Relations Board issuing a series of rulings that penalized Amazon for its conduct during bargaining.

Warehouse workers at YVR2, the Amazon fulfilment centre in Delta, B.C., were first granted union certification by the board in July 2025. It ordered remedial certification (meaning that certification was granted without a vote) because it ruled that Amazon made a fair workplace vote impossible by rapidly boosting the number of new hires during the union drive.

For more than a year after the certification, Unifor and Amazon continued to disagree on terms of a new contract, with the union pushing for clauses that could address how fast workers are expected to work, and Amazon refusing to negotiate on worker productivity. Multiple unfair labour practice complaints were filed by the union against Amazon at the board. Then, in early August, the board again ruled against Amazon, saying that it had bargained in bad faith and was unwilling to negotiate on key items. The board ordered a first contract to be imposed on workers.

“The fact that this first contract had to come through arbitration is not great. It is a bit of a challenge for a union when the members themselves did not have direct input on the terms of the agreement,” said Adam King, assistant professor of labour studies at the University of Manitoba.

Bethany Hastie, director of the Centre for Law in the Contemporary Workplace at Queen’s University, said that ideally, the unionization process should not unfold with a labour board imposing arbitration but that these safeguards are in place for a reason.

“Labour boards exist to ensure fairness for workers who want to unionize. With this case, as it has proceeded, the labour board was attuned to the various ways in which the employer tried to undermine labour rights in the workplace.”

In January 2025, Amazon closed all seven of its warehouses and distribution facilities in Quebec, terminating 1,700 full-time employees. The company said it was a business decision. But the move came just months after its facility in Laval, Que., had voted to unionize and was on the verge of securing a first contract. At the time, labour experts and local politicians speculated that the closures were linked to the unionization and other union drives in Amazon facilities across the province.

Prof. King believes that Amazon is unlikely to shut down its Vancouver operations because they are too geographically important for the company. “In the case of Quebec, they had already shifted their network to rely on serving other geographic markets from the Greater Toronto Area,” he said.

Mr. McGarrigle, of Unifor, said it’s a big win for the workers the union represents, who can now enter a grievance process if they believe their working conditions have been violated. “This is particularly important at Amazon, where the worker injury rate is high,” he said.

Separately, a group of workers at the Delta fulfilment centre has been trying to decertify the union for months. Unifor believes Amazon is involved in the decertification drive, and has filed an unfair labour practice complaint at the provincial labour board. These workers have also filed a judicial review at the B.C. Supreme Court over an order by the labour board to seal the results of their decertification vote. No decision has been made on the issue.
summary: The 800-odd workers now have seat at the table to challenge company on safety issues, Unifor regional director says
